text: Education in the Republic begins with stories, since children hear them before they ever train their bodies (377a). The founders must therefore supervise the makers of stories, and in Book II Socrates lays down two laws for what may be said about the gods. The first: God is good, and so the cause of good things only. The evils of the world far outnumber the goods, and another cause must be found for them, because nothing good can do harm (379b–c). The second: God neither changes nor deceives (380d–383a). Whatever is in the best condition is least altered from outside, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse. Three kinds of story are excluded: Homer's two jars at the threshold of Zeus (379d), any poet who blames a god for a ruined house, and every tale of a god who changes his shape. The lie that gods and human beings hate most is the lie in the soul, worse than the spoken one. It is the condition of being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself (382a–b). A god has no such lie within, and no motive to plant one in anyone else.
